problem: Existing ObjectNav methods rely on static symbolic priors, limited memory, or isolated components. They lack dynamic graph updates, failure-aware replanning and real-robot validation, so they struggle with occlusion, ambiguous targets and long-horizon search.
motivation: Robots in cluttered, partially observable homes must combine perception, symbolic reasoning and spatial planning. Occluded goals can be reached indirectly through co-occurring anchor objects (e.g. laptop via desk/chair), so a system that chains such anchors over a semantic grid could be both efficient and interpretable.
key_idea: Build an online open-vocabulary scene graph and semantic occupancy grid, chain co-occurrence-derived relay anchors as subgoals, execute them with A*/D* and learned goal-conditioned control, and optionally use an LLM to revise failing anchor chains.
insight: The ablation on RoboTHOR shows the symbolic relay components carry most of the performance. Removing the co-occurrence graph cuts SR from 85.64 to 42.56, removing relay chaining gives 40.00, and random relay objects give 34.18, so the gains come from meaningful semantic anchors. The headline numbers are obtained with the LLM introspection disabled, so its contribution is untested. The oracle static grid reaches 95.38 SR, showing that egocentric mapping is a remaining bottleneck.
method: DovSG (dynamic open-vocabulary scene graph): nodes carry label, embedding, 3D position and box; edges carry a relation and a spatial-affinity score. Graph updates match detections by embedding similarity plus position, and stale nodes are pruned. Language queries are grounded by label similarity plus graph context.

Co-occurrence relay planning: a weighted object co-occurrence graph is clustered by modularity. Relay chains maximize summed edge weights from start anchor to goal, optionally mixed with LLM-proposed candidates via a beta-weighted score.
Semantic occupancy grid and planning: a multi-hot semantic grid is built from RGB-D (sim) or LiDAR+IMU (real). It is used for reachability checks of anchors and A*/D* path planning with replanning.

Transformer behavioral cloning subgoal decomposition: an encoder-decoder predicts (action, object) subgoals from instruction, scene graph and co-occurrence prior. Subgoals are fused with the prior and filtered by grounding, feasibility and redundancy checks.

Goal-conditioned RL (GCRL, GRIP-F): a PPO policy conditioned on a subgoal embedding, RGB-D, pose, DovSG features and the local map. The reward combines goal, progress, collision and drift terms, trained with a curriculum.

LLM introspection and recovery: on failure, GPT-4o (or similar) receives visited anchors and the scene graph and proposes revised anchors. These are filtered by the grid and applied through a soft reset.
Variants: GRIP-L (AI2-THOR, static chaining, no LLM), GRIP-F (RoboTHOR, full), GRIP-R (Jetbot Pro real robot with YOLOv8, RPLIDAR, IMU).

setting.backbone: Transformer BC subgoal predictor + PPO goal-conditioned policy + YOLOv8 detector; GPT-4o for introspection (disabled in reported RoboTHOR results)
setting.training_data: Expert-annotated subgoal demonstrations for BC and PPO in simulation with curriculum, using AI2-THOR (75 train scenes) and RoboTHOR (AllenAct ObjectNav split 60 train scenes); dataset scale not given
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB-D (simulation, ground-truth depth in AI2-THOR); monocular RGB + 2D LiDAR + IMU on the real robot
setting.action_space: Discrete low-level actions (forward, turn, interact) in simulation; real robot uses Move Forward 10 cm / Rotate ±90°; symbolic subgoals (goto, inspect, interact)
setting.privileged: Ground-truth depth in AI2-THOR; the co-occurrence graph is built from scene statistics; the 'Static Grid (Oracle)' ablation uses a full map, not the main method

numbers_note: Simulation splits are ambiguous: the paper never says which of the val/test splits the tables use. The AI2-THOR and RoboTHOR benchmarks are non-standard (custom SAE metric, 1 m success radius). Object-wise results appear only in figures. The ablation (Table 6) gives SR/SPL/SAE for RoboTHOR variants: w/o co-occurrence 42.56/28.93/20.41, w/o relay chaining 40.00/29.08/27.70, random relay 34.18/23.92/18.01, oracle static grid 95.38/94.69/73.01.
results: GRIP-F reaches 85.64 SR / 61.03 SPL / 67.06 SAE on RoboTHOR versus the strongest baseline Zheng et al. (76.00/40.94/42.89). GRIP-L gets 84.10 SR (below Zheng et al., 87.69) but 63.48 SPL and 91.79 SR / 93.88 SPL on L>=5. On a real Jetbot, SR is 86.67–100% across five objects with 15 trials each.
limitations: No visibility filtering or anchor confidence scoring, so occluded or unreachable anchors cause failures; LLM introspection was not evaluated in the reported results even though it is claimed as a key contribution.

Real-world evaluation is a single apartment with 5 objects and no baselines; sim splits and baseline protocols are unclear, and the very high SPL/SAE (e.g. 93.88 on L>=5, above SR) and the abstract's '>30%' claim are not clearly consistent with the tables.
GRIP-R relies on static priors without LLM replanning, and an oracle-grid ablation shows a large gap from egocentric mapping.
